title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: I sat one evening in my laboratory. The sun had set. The moon was just rising from the sea. I didn't have enough light to work and sat idle, debating whether to stop for the night or push on to finish. As I sat, a chain of thoughts led me to consider the consequences of what I was doing. Three years ago, I'd been engaged in the same kind of work and had created a fiend whose unparalleled cruelty had devastated my heart and filled it forever with the bitterest remorse. Now I was about to create another being whose character was equally unknown to me. She might become ten thousand times more malicious than her mate and delight in murder and misery for their own sake. He had sworn to leave humanity and hide in the wilderness, but she hadn't made any such promise. She would in all likelihood become a thinking, reasoning being and might refuse to honor a deal made before she existed. They might even hate each other. The creature already loathed his own ugliness — might he not feel even greater revulsion seeing it mirrored in a female form? She might also reject him and be drawn to the superior beauty of humans. She might leave him, and he'd be alone again — enraged by the fresh provocation of being abandoned by one of his own kind.

Even if they left Europe and lived in the wilderness, one of the first results of the companionship the demon craved would be children. A race of devils would spread across the earth, who might make the very existence of the human species precarious and terrifying. Did I have the right, for my own benefit, to inflict this curse on all future generations? I'd been swayed before by the sly arguments of the being I had created. I'd been paralyzed by his fiendish threats. But now, for the first time, the wickedness of my promise struck me with full force. I shuddered to think that future ages might curse me as their plague — someone whose selfishness had bought his own peace at the price, perhaps, of the entire human race's survival.

I trembled. My courage failed. Looking up, I saw by moonlight the demon at the window. A ghastly grin twisted his lips as he watched me working at the task he'd assigned. Yes — he had followed me on my travels. He'd lurked in forests, hidden in caves, and camped on empty moors. Now he'd come to check my progress and claim the fulfillment of my promise.

As I looked at him — his face expressing the most extreme malice and treachery — I thought with something like madness of my promise to create another like him. Trembling with passion, I tore to pieces the thing I'd been working on. The wretch saw me destroy the creature on whose future existence his happiness depended. With a howl of devilish despair and revenge, he withdrew.

I left the room, locked the door, and made a solemn vow in my heart never to resume this work. Then, with trembling steps, I made my way to my own room. I was alone. No one was near to ease the gloom or free me from my terrible thoughts.

Several hours passed. I stood near my window, gazing at the sea. It was almost motionless. The wind had died. All nature rested under the quiet moon's gaze. A few fishing boats dotted the water. Now and then a gentle breeze carried the sound of fishermen calling to each other. I felt the silence without being fully conscious of how deep it was — until suddenly my ear caught the sound of oars paddling near the shore and someone landing close to my house.

A few minutes later, I heard the creak of my door, as if someone were trying to open it quietly. I trembled from head to foot. I sensed who it was and wanted to rouse one of the peasants living in a nearby cottage. But I was paralyzed — gripped by that helplessness you feel in nightmares when you try to flee from danger and cannot move.
Soon I heard footsteps in the passage. The door opened. The wretch I dreaded appeared. Closing the door, he approached me and said in a muffled voice,

"You've destroyed the work you began. What do you intend? Do you dare break your promise? I've endured suffering and misery. I left Switzerland with you. I crept along the banks of the Rhine, through its willow islands and over the summits of its hills. I've lived for months on the moors of England and in the wilds of Scotland. I've endured unimaginable exhaustion, cold, and hunger. Do you dare destroy my hopes?"
"Go away! I am breaking my promise. I will never create another like you — equal in ugliness and evil."

"Slave! I tried to reason with you before, but you've proven yourself unworthy of my patience. Remember that I have power. You think yourself miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!"

"My time of hesitation is over. Now the time of your power has come. Your threats can't force me to commit evil. They only confirm my decision not to create you a companion in wickedness. Shall I deliberately unleash another demon upon the earth, one whose pleasure is death and destruction? Get out! I am firm. Your words will only increase my rage."

The monster saw my resolve in my face and gnashed his teeth with helpless anger. "Shall every man," he cried, "find a wife, and every animal have its mate, while I remain alone? I had feelings of love and tenderness, and they were met with hatred and scorn. Man! You may hate me, but beware! Your hours will be spent in dread and misery. Soon the blow will fall that will destroy your happiness forever. Are you to be happy while I suffer in the depths of wretchedness? You can crush my other passions, but revenge remains — revenge, now dearer to me than light or food! I may die, but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that shines on your misery. Be warned, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I'll watch with the cunning of a snake, ready to strike with its venom. Man, you shall pay for the wrongs you inflict."
"Devil, stop! Don't poison the air with your malice. I've stated my decision, and I'm no coward to back down before words. Leave me. I won't be moved."
"Very well. I go. But remember — I shall be with you on your wedding night."
I lunged forward and cried, "Villain! Before you sign my death warrant, make sure you are yourself safe."
I would have seized him, but he dodged me and fled the house. Moments later I saw him in his boat, which shot across the water with the speed of an arrow and was soon lost among the waves.

Everything was silent again, but his words rang in my ears. I burned with rage. I wanted to chase the murderer of my peace and hurl him into the ocean. I paced my room, wild and agitated, while my imagination conjured a thousand tormenting images. Why hadn't I followed him and fought him to the death? But I had let him go, and he was heading toward the mainland. I shuddered to think who might be the next victim sacrificed to his insatiable revenge. Then I thought again of his words: "_I will be with you on your wedding night._" That, then, was when my fate would be sealed. On that night I would die, satisfying and ending his hatred. The prospect didn't frighten me. But when I thought of my beloved Elizabeth — her tears and endless grief when she found her lover so brutally taken from her — tears came to my eyes, the first I'd shed in months. I resolved not to fall before my enemy without a bitter fight.

The night passed. The sun rose from the ocean. My feelings became calmer — if you can call it calm when the violence of rage sinks into the depths of despair. I left the house, the scene of last night's confrontation, and walked on the beach. I almost saw the sea as an impassable barrier between me and my fellow human beings — and part of me wished it were true. I wanted to spend the rest of my life on that barren rock, wearily but undisturbed by sudden shocks of tragedy. If I went back, I would either be killed or watch those I loved most die in the grip of a demon I myself had made.

I walked the island like a restless ghost, cut off from everything I loved and wretched in the separation. When noon came and the sun climbed higher, I lay down on the grass and was overcome by deep sleep. I'd been awake all the previous night. My nerves were strained. My eyes were inflamed from stress and sleeplessness. The sleep refreshed me. When I woke, I felt again as if I belonged to a race of human beings like myself and began to reflect on what had happened with more composure. Yet the fiend's words still rang in my ears like a death knell. They seemed like a dream, yet as distinct and oppressive as reality.

The sun had descended far when I still sat on the shore, eating an oat cake to satisfy my ravenous hunger. Then I saw a fishing boat land nearby. One of the men brought me a packet of letters from Geneva, along with one from Clerval begging me to join him. He said he was wasting his time where he was. Letters from friends he'd made in London asked him to return to complete negotiations for his India venture. He couldn't delay his departure any longer. Since his London trip might soon be followed by the longer voyage to India, he begged me to spend as much time with him as I could spare. He asked me to leave my solitary island and meet him at Perth so we could travel south together. This letter partly recalled me to life. I decided to leave the island in two days.

But before I left, there was one task I dreaded: I had to pack up my chemical instruments, which meant entering the room where I'd done my hideous work and handling equipment that sickened me. The next morning at dawn, I summoned enough courage and unlocked the laboratory door. The remains of the half-finished creature lay scattered on the floor. I almost felt as if I'd dismembered a living human being. I paused to collect myself, then entered. With trembling hands I carried the instruments out. But I realized I shouldn't leave the remains behind to horrify the islanders and arouse suspicion. I put them in a basket with a large quantity of stones. I planned to throw the basket into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach, cleaning and arranging my chemical equipment.

Nothing could be more complete than the change in my feelings since the night the demon appeared. Before, I'd viewed my promise with gloomy despair as something that must be fulfilled no matter what. Now I felt as if a veil had been lifted from my eyes. I could see clearly for the first time. The idea of resuming my work didn't even cross my mind. The threat I'd heard weighed on me, but I didn't consider that any voluntary act of mine could prevent it. I'd decided in my own heart that creating another like the fiend I had first made would be an act of the basest, most atrocious selfishness. I banished from my mind every thought that might lead to a different conclusion.

Between two and three in the morning, the moon rose. I put my basket in a small boat and sailed out about four miles from shore. The scene was perfectly solitary. A few boats were heading toward land, but I sailed away from them. I felt as if I were about to commit a terrible crime and shrank from encountering anyone. When the moon, which had been clear, was suddenly covered by a thick cloud, I seized the moment of darkness and dropped my basket into the sea. I listened to the gurgling sound as it sank, then sailed away. The sky clouded over, but the air was pure though chilled by a rising northeast wind. It refreshed me and filled me with surprisingly pleasant feelings. I decided to extend my time on the water. Fixing the rudder in a straight position, I stretched out at the bottom of the boat. Clouds hid the moon. Everything was dark. I heard only the sound of the keel cutting through water. The murmur lulled me, and soon I was deeply asleep.

I don't know how long I slept, but when I woke, the sun was already high. The wind was strong. Waves threatened my little boat's safety. I realized the wind was from the northeast and must have driven me far from the coast I'd set out from. I tried to change course but quickly found that doing so would swamp the boat. My only option was to run before the wind. I confess I felt a flash of terror. I had no compass. I knew so little of this region's geography that the sun was useless to me. I might be driven into the open Atlantic and face starvation, or be swallowed by the enormous waves roaring around me. I'd been adrift for many hours already. I felt the torment of burning thirst — a preview of worse suffering to come. I looked up at the sky, covered by clouds racing before the wind. I looked at the sea. It would be my grave. "Fiend," I cried, "your task is already done!" I thought of Elizabeth, of my father, of Clerval — all left behind, on whom the monster might now satisfy his bloodthirsty, merciless passions. This thought plunged me into such despairing, frightful imagination that even now, as the scene is about to close before me forever, I shudder to think of it.

Hours passed. But gradually, as the sun descended, the wind dropped to a gentle breeze and the sea grew calmer. Heavy swells replaced the breakers. I felt seasick and could barely hold the rudder — when suddenly I saw a line of high land to the south.
Nearly spent with exhaustion and the terrible suspense of the last several hours, this sudden certainty of survival rushed to my heart like a flood of warm joy. Tears streamed from my eyes.

How changeable our feelings are! And how strange is our clinging love of life, even in the worst misery! I made another sail from part of my clothing and eagerly steered toward land. It looked wild and rocky, but as I drew closer, I could see signs of farming. I spotted boats near the shore and found myself suddenly back in the world of civilization. I carefully followed the coastline and spotted a church steeple rising from behind a small headland. Since I was in a state of extreme weakness, I headed straight for the town as the likeliest place to find food. Fortunately, I had money with me. As I rounded the headland, I saw a small, tidy town with a good harbor, which I entered, my heart leaping with joy at my unexpected escape.

While I was busy securing my boat and arranging the sail, several people gathered around me. They seemed very surprised by my appearance. Instead of offering help, they whispered together with gestures that might have alarmed me under other circumstances. As it was, I merely noticed they spoke English and addressed them in that language. "My good friends," I said, "would you kindly tell me the name of this town and where I am?"
"You'll know that soon enough," replied a man with a harsh voice. "Maybe you've come to a place that won't be to your liking. But you won't be asked about your lodgings, I promise you."

I was extremely surprised to get such a rude answer from a stranger, and I was also unsettled to see the frowning, angry faces of his companions. "Why do you speak to me so roughly?" I replied. "Surely it's not the English custom to receive strangers so inhospitably."
"I don't know about the English custom," said the man, "but it's the Irish custom to hate villains."

As this strange exchange continued, the crowd grew rapidly. Their faces showed a mix of curiosity and anger that annoyed and somewhat alarmed me. I asked for directions to the inn, but no one answered. I moved forward. A murmur rose from the crowd as they followed and surrounded me. Then a rough-looking man tapped me on the shoulder and said, "Come, sir. You must follow me to Mr. Kirwin's to give an account of yourself."
"Who is Mr. Kirwin? Why must I give an account of myself? Isn't this a free country?"
"Aye, sir — free enough for honest folk. Mr. Kirwin is the magistrate. You're to give an account of the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night."

This answer startled me, but I quickly recovered. I was innocent. That could easily be proved. So I followed my escort in silence and was led to one of the best houses in town. I was ready to collapse from exhaustion and hunger. But surrounded by a crowd, I thought it wise to summon all my strength, so that physical weakness wouldn't be mistaken for guilt or fear. Little did I know that within minutes, a catastrophe would overwhelm me and, in horror and despair, extinguish all fear of shame or death.
I must pause here. It takes all my strength to recall the terrible events I'm about to describe in proper detail.
